report.board_note: The board is fragmented, not unified: bullion and copper are pointing one way and energy the other. GOLD's implied open is -0.39%, SILVER's is -4.64% and COPPER's is -4.20%, while CRUDEOIL's is +7.53% and NATURALGAS's is +1.21% - a split book, not a single overnight theme. The rupee is a bystander today, not the story: usd/inr moved 0.79% (95.5961 vs a prior 94.85122, TWELVE_DATA, as_of 2026-09-10 against a prior read of 2026-09-08) while the reference legs on copper, silver and crude each moved several percentage points overnight - the rupee is too small to explain moves an order of magnitude larger, so these are reference-led opens, not currency-led ones. None of the five Tier A implied opens are actually overnight moves: every one of them carries the label "over 2 calendar days - NOT overnight", even though each instrument's own international reference leg was a one-day, overnight move - the compound is only as fast as its slowest leg, and here the rupee leg is the one spanning two calendar days. Four of the nine instruments - ZINC, ALUMINIUM, LEAD and NICKEL - carry no implied open at all, by design: LME publishes before MCX closes, so an overnight reference window does not exist for them. On the bullion premium, GOLD sits 1.25 percentage points below import parity with a z of -0.13 over 198 sessions - an ordinary discount - while SILVER sits 3.03 points above parity with a z of 0.29 over 218 sessions; neither reading is extreme for its own instrument, so the size of the two-legged fall in SILVER's implied open is not being amplified by an unusual premium.

report.board_note: The board carries no stored news items at all for this run — no headline array reached this agent for any of the nine instruments, so there is nothing to read against the tape this morning. There is also no DXY row on the board, so the dollar cannot be characterised one way or the other. Four instruments show large implied-open moves (COPPER -4.2%, SILVER -4.64%, CRUDEOIL +7.53%, NATURALGAS +1.21%, all measured over a two-calendar-day span rather than overnight) with nothing in the news feed to explain any of them; that gap is the single most notable fact in this pass — the moves, if real, are positioning- or international-reference-leg-led, not story-led. Base metals (ALUMINIUM, ZINC, LEAD, NICKEL) have no implied-open leg at all (Tier B) and, as expected, no coverage either.

report.board_note: Five of nine instruments — gold, copper, aluminium, lead and zinc — are marked LONG_LIQUIDATION this morning: positions unwinding rather than fresh conviction on either side. The unwind is large relative to the book in the base metals — aluminium's open interest fell by 445 contracts against a total of 3,826, zinc's by 259 against 2,356, copper's by 1,062 against 10,292 — against gold's comparatively small 221-contract decline against a total of 10,187, and lead's 19-contract decline against 677. That lean is not universal. Crude oil is marked NEW_LONGS on a 2,822-contract rise against a total of 19,973, the largest single open-interest change on the board, while natural gas is marked NEW_SHORTS on a 3,512-contract rise against a total of 56,751 — so the energy complex is split between fresh buying and fresh selling rather than aligned with each other or with the metals. Silver, sitting in the same bullion complex as gold, is also marked NEW_SHORTS (open interest up 901 contracts against a total of 13,213) rather than liquidation — fresh selling, not an exit, even though both gold and silver show a negative overnight reference move. Nickel stands alone as SHORT_COVERING, an open-interest change of -77 contracts against a small total of 346 — the largest change relative to its own book on the board. Two of the nine reads carry an internal contradiction the board does not resolve: natural gas's NEW_SHORTS label implies a lower local close even as its overnight international reference (+0.43%) and its two-day implied open (+1.21%, not itself an overnight figure) both show a positive move, and nickel's SHORT_COVERING label implies a higher local close while its LME reference for the same session moved -0.36% lower. On COT, natural gas sits at the very top of its range (1.0) and aluminium close behind (0.9311, carried with a weak correlation-to-price caveat as Tier B proxy data), while lead (0.0) and copper (0.104) sit at the extreme bottom — a crowded-short signal on two separate legs, the more predictive extreme by the board's own asymmetry. Overall the board is fragmented, not aligned: liquidation dominates the gold/base-metal cluster, but crude, natural gas and silver are each adding fresh positioning in different directions, and two of the nine instruments show a positioning label that does not square with their own reference price move.

report.board_note: Six of the nine instruments sit within one ATR of a level - GOLD's support at 0.93 ATR, SILVER's support at 0.42 ATR, COPPER's support at 0.66 ATR, ZINC's resistance at 0.89 ATR, LEAD's support at 0.62 ATR and NICKEL's support at 0.45 ATR - so the board reads coiled rather than adrift. The remaining three sit further out: NATURALGAS at 1.27 ATR to support, ALUMINIUM at 1.53 ATR to support, and CRUDEOIL at 2.52 ATR to its only stated level. Volatility is not uniform across that coiled group: GOLD's range of 2,880.86 against a recent average of 2,708.68, and ZINC's range of 10.06 against 7.43, are both running meaningfully above their own averages - expanding. SILVER (5,390.71 vs 5,871.88), CRUDEOIL (305.36 vs 356.80), ALUMINIUM (4.44 vs 5.16) and LEAD (1.60 vs 2.51) are all running below their own averages - compressed. NATURALGAS (8.73 vs 8.78), COPPER (17.53 vs 16.65) and NICKEL (20.29 vs 20.84) sit close enough to their own averages to call unremarkable. The exceptions worth naming are GOLD and ZINC together: each combines a level under one ATR away with a range that is itself expanding, the only two instruments on the board where nearness and volatility point the same direction at once. Everywhere else, a close level sits against compressed or unremarkable volatility, or a level sits too far out for volatility to matter. On the cross-instrument ratios: gold sits at 65.08 rupees-per-gram of silver, both legs normalised for MCX's differing gold (10 gram) and silver (1 kilogram) quoting, at the 52.86th percentile of a 250-session back-adjusted continuous window - unremarkable positioning in the metal ratio even while SILVER itself runs a compressed range.
